articles.title: A school report card for your website: security headers, e-mail protection and certificate, graded like at school
articles.excerpt: Try it first: type a domain into the report card, wait a few seconds, and you get a school report for that website. There is a demo button with my own site, which gets an A. Security headers (40 %): H…
articles.body: Try it first: type a domain into the report card , wait a few seconds, and you get a school report for that website. There is a demo button with my own site, which gets an A. What is graded Security headers (40 %): HSTS, Content-Security-Policy, nosniff, frame protection, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy, COOP and whether the server gives away its version. Same scoring as the header checker . E-mail protection (35 %): SPF and how it ends ( -all or ~all ), DMARC and its policy (reject, quarantine or none), DMARC reports and MTA-STS. This decides how easily someone can send forged mail in your domain's name. TLS certificate (25 %): valid, trusted, matching the name, days left and the protocol version.

articles.title: Laravel Queue Worker on cPanel Without Supervisor
articles.excerpt: The Laravel docs tell you to keep queue:work running with Supervisor. On cPanel shared hosting you cannot install it, so emails, PDFs and imports sit in the jobs table and never run. This guide shows…
articles.body: The Laravel docs tell you to keep queue:work running with Supervisor. On cPanel shared hosting you cannot install it, so emails, PDFs and imports sit in the jobs table and never run. This guide shows two ways to run a Laravel queue worker on cPanel without Supervisor: a cron job every minute that starts a worker and lets it exit, or the same worker started by Laravel's scheduler. Both stay inside CloudLinux limits if you set the options correctly. Quick answer: use the database queue driver, then add one cPanel cron job that runs every minute: cd /home/USERNAME/app && /opt/cpanel/ea-php83/root/usr/bin/php artisan queue:work --stop-when-empty --max-time=50 --tries=3 --timeout=45 >/dev/null 2>&1 .

articles.body: Static code analysis is an important part of modern software engineering. It helps teams identify potential bugs, security vulnerabilities, code smells, and maintainability issues before they reach production. But I’ve always wondered: does running static analysis really need to be complicated? There are excellent tools available, including SonarQube and Semgrep. However, depending on your requirements, adopting them can involve additional infrastructure, configuration, and ongoing maintenance. I wanted to explore a simpler approach. That’s how Sonda started. Today, I’m sharing version 0.2.1 of Sonda, an open-source static analysis tool written in Rust. And I’m looking for developers willing to put it to the test. What is Sonda?

articles.title: Why TDS stays high after a bonus: how Indian payroll engines recalculate salary tax
articles.excerpt: After a large bonus, payroll gets the same ticket every year: "My bonus was paid last month. Why is TDS still high this month?" The engine is almost always right. Indian payroll systems project tax fo…
articles.body: After a large bonus, payroll gets the same ticket every year: "My bonus was paid last month. Why is TDS still high this month?" The engine is almost always right. Indian payroll systems project tax for the whole year, subtract what has already been deducted, and spread the balance over the months that are left. A bonus raises the projection, so the deduction stays higher for the rest of the year, bonus or no bonus. The example below walks through the numbers so engineers and payroll ops can debug these tickets from the formula itself. How payroll engines calculate monthly TDS on salary Most Indian payroll systems use the same three steps every month. First, estimate the employee's tax for the full tax year from salary paid so far, salary still expected, and any one-time income.

articles.title: 48-Hour Field Notes: My Client Timed Out, the Server Finished the Work, and My Batch Ran Twice
articles.excerpt: Two nights ago my batch job wrote 200 rows and I expected 200 rows. What I got was 261, and nothing in the logs said "error" — just a scattering of timeouts I had trained myself to ignore. So here is…
articles.body: Two nights ago my batch job wrote 200 rows and I expected 200 rows. What I got was 261, and nothing in the logs said "error" — just a scattering of timeouts I had trained myself to ignore. So here is the question I should have asked 48 hours earlier: when my HTTP client gives up, who told the server to stop? Nobody did. That is the whole article, but the interesting part is how quietly it happens, and what a cheap harness looks like that would have caught it before the nightly run. What the logs actually showed My worker logged timeout after 3.0s and moved on to the next item, which felt like normal resilience at the time. The remote side, meanwhile, kept generating, finished at roughly 5.5 seconds, and returned a perfectly good result to a socket nobody was reading anymore.

articles.title: How I Taught a Billing Desk to Remember with Hindsight
articles.excerpt: How I Taught a Billing Desk to Remember with Hindsight A hospital billing desk denied a dengue claim worth ₹1,45,000. The reason was one line: "OPD-convertible." The desk appealed the way it always ha…
articles.body: How I Taught a Billing Desk to Remember with Hindsight A hospital billing desk denied a dengue claim worth ₹1,45,000. The reason was one line: "OPD-convertible." The desk appealed the way it always had — a generic letter, no evidence attached. The appeal failed. Six months later, the same desk denied another dengue claim for the same reason, and appealed it the same way. It failed again. Nothing was wrong with the desk's intentions. What was missing was memory. The problem is not the denial. It is the forgetting. Indian hospital TPA desks process thousands of claims. Insurers deny them on a handful of recurring patterns: hospitalization "not justified", pre-existing disease invoked against an unrelated illness, room-rent caps, delayed intimation, non-payable items.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 6, 1572: A German astronomer discovers the Tycho supernova with the naked eye, but everyone thought the cosmic explosion was a 'new star'
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 6, 1572, the German astronomer Wolfgang Schulër observed a supernova later caleld the Tycho supernova with his bare eyes. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 6, 1572, the German astronomer Wolfgang Schulër observed a supernova with his bare eyes. He spotted the exploding star in the constellation Cassiopeia. It was as bright as Venus and could even be seen during the day. Astronomers were really confused, because it looked like a star just appeared out of nowhere. Schulër may have been the first to see it, but the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe is widely credited for the discovery. Brahe studied it in detail and wrote a whole book about this so-called "new star." It then became known as "Tycho's Star." At the time, supernovas had not yet been discovered. Tycho's Star was finally classified as a supernova in the 1940s. Scientists now think it was a small star called a white dwarf that exploded thousands of years ago.

articles.excerpt: AST SpaceMobile plans to launch its broadband satellites on a new rocket called Blacklift, which it will build in house and plans to start flying in 2028.
articles.body: Another new private rocket is in the works. AST SpaceMobile announced today (Nov. 6) that it's building a reusable rocket called Blacklift to launch its broadband satellites to low Earth orbit (LEO), with first flight targeted in 2028. The news comes just 10 days after Cowboy Space unveiled Big Iron , a rocket designed to launch its constellation of 20,000 AI data centers . Cowboy Space is also targeting 2028 for its first liftoff. "The Blacklift rocket is the springboard to significantly expand our total addressable market, providing AST SpaceMobile with regular unconstrained access to orbit and providing for most favorable owners’ economics in the industry," Abel Avellan, the company's founder, chairman and CEO, said in a statement today .

articles.title: What's that bright 'star' in the early morning sky? It's not a star at all!
articles.excerpt: Spotted a dazzling light in the eastern sky before sunrise? It's Venus, and the planet is only going to get brighter as it heads toward its spectacular peak later this month.
articles.body: Early morning risers heading to work or school before sunrise are likely to notice a very bright, star-like object appearing low in the east-southeast sky just before sunrise. What is somewhat amazing is that just a couple of weeks ago this object wasn't there at all, but now it literally stands out with such brilliance as to almost command the attention of commuters who might be traveling in an easterly direction to "Look at me!" The object in question is, of course, the planet Venus, which is currently amid one of its most spectacular forays into the morning sky, literally "vaulting up" into prominence. On Oct. 24, Venus came to inferior conjunction, passing between the Earth and sun and shifting from the evening into the morning sky.

articles.title: Chainalysis says hackers stole credentials and tokens for all of its customers
articles.excerpt: Company said a "multifront cyberattack" included AI agents and an on-path data snatch.
articles.body: Blockchain analysis firm Chainalysis said that hackers have obtained sensitive personal information—including names, usernames, password hashes, and live tokens—for all of its users following a breach of its network security. The accomplishment could be a major coup for the attackers. Both Chainalysis and public sources have revealed a long list of high-profile customers, including government agencies such as the FBI, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency, and the US Air Force, as well as private companies such as Microsoft, Coinbase, and Barclays. It's unclear if the data theft exposed customers to additional threats. We regret to inform you...

articles.title: I finally got my hands on the Unistellar Envision smart binoculars with augmented reality and I can’t wait to stargaze with them
articles.excerpt: The Unistellar Envision smart binoculars have an augmented reality (AR) overlay that provides smart functionality to 10x50 binoculars, enabling night sky and landmark identification.
articles.body: I have been waiting to get my hands on a pair of Unistellar Envision smart binoculars since they were announced in 2024. Our editor-in-chief tried an early demo of them last year and said that they felt like something out of Star Trek . He was, of course, referencing the red augmented reality (AR) overlay in the Envisions that can identify night sky targets and landmarks, as well as displaying navigational tools. These are the first pair of smart binoculars that can identify targets in the night sky, such as planets, stars and deep space objects. The build is solid and while they aren't the most lightweight binoculars , the body is hiding that extra technology that enables the AR overlay in the right hand lens.
